questions.prompt: Why is memory arranged as a hierarchy rather than as one large fast memory?
options: Because programs cannot address more than a few megabytes
Because fast memory is expensive per byte, so only a little of it is affordable
Because the CPU can only talk to one memory at a time
Because the operating system requires it
questions.explanation: Speed costs money and space. The hierarchy buys the illusion of a memory that is both large and fast by keeping the data currently in use in the small fast levels.

questions.prompt: A program reads an array from start to end. Which principle makes the cache effective here?
questions.explanation: Spatial locality: addresses close to one just used are likely to be used soon. A cache line brings in several neighbouring words at once, so one miss pays for many hits.

options: Every write goes to cache and to memory at the same time
Writes go only to the cache; memory is updated when the line is evicted
Writes are buffered and discarded on a miss
questions.explanation: Write-back delays the memory write until eviction, which saves bus traffic when a line is written repeatedly. The cost is a dirty bit per line and a harder time keeping multiple caches coherent.

questions.prompt: A cache has a 95% hit rate, 1 ns hit time and 100 ns miss penalty. What is the average access time?
questions.explanation: 1 + 0.05 x 100 = 6 ns. The lesson is how heavily the rare miss dominates: at a 95% hit rate the cache is still six times slower than its hit time, and going from 95% to 99% cuts the average to a third (1 + 0.01 x 100 = 2 ns).

questions.prompt: Increasing the cache line size always improves the hit rate.
options: True: more data is fetched per miss
False: beyond a point it wastes bandwidth and evicts useful data
True, provided the cache is direct-mapped
False, because line size cannot be changed
questions.explanation: Longer lines exploit spatial locality up to a point, but a fixed-size cache then holds fewer lines, so unrelated data is evicted sooner and each miss transfers more bytes the program may never touch. The hit rate curve turns back down.

questions.prompt: In a direct-mapped cache, how many places can a given memory block be stored?
questions.explanation: Direct-mapped means the block's address decides its line. It is the cheapest to build and the fastest to look up, but two hot blocks that map to the same line will evict each other for ever - a conflict miss.

questions.prompt: A direct-mapped cache has 4 lines of 2 words. The program reads address 0, then 16, then 0, then 16, and so on. What happens?
options: Only the first two accesses miss
It depends on the replacement policy
questions.explanation: Blocks 0 and 8 both map to line 0 (8 mod 4 = 0), so each access throws the other block out: every access is a miss, and all but the first two are conflict misses. A 2-way cache keeps both, and replacement policy does not matter in a direct-mapped cache because there is only ever one candidate line. Try it in the lesson with the Ping-pong preset.

questions.prompt: Which kind of miss can no cache design avoid?
options: None - a big enough cache avoids them all
questions.explanation: The first access to a block always misses: it has never been in the cache. More lines remove capacity misses, more associativity removes conflict misses, but only prefetching or bigger blocks can soften compulsory ones.

questions.prompt: Which memory has to be refreshed constantly or it forgets its contents, even with power on?
questions.explanation: DRAM keeps each bit as charge on a tiny capacitor, which leaks; every row is rewritten roughly every 64 ms. That one-transistor-one-capacitor cell is why DRAM is dense and cheap, and the refresh plus the read sensing is part of why it is slow. SRAM uses six transistors per bit and holds its value as long as it has power.

questions.prompt: 32-bit byte addresses, a direct-mapped cache of 1024 lines, 16-byte blocks. How many bits are in the tag?
questions.explanation: Offset: log2(16) = 4 bits. Index: log2(1024) = 10 bits. Tag: whatever is left, 32 - 10 - 4 = 18. Always find offset and index first; the tag is the remainder.

questions.prompt: If one nanosecond were stretched to one second, roughly how long would a single hard-disk access (about 10 ms) take?
questions.explanation: 10 ms is 10,000,000 ns, so 10,000,000 s - about 116 days. On the same scale an L1 hit is one second and a RAM access is over a minute. That gap is the whole reason the hierarchy exists.

questions.prompt: A fully associative LRU cache always has a miss rate no worse than a direct-mapped cache of the same size.
options: False: for some access patterns it does worse
True: it can put any block anywhere
True, but only with blocks of one word
False: fully associative caches have no replacement policy
questions.explanation: Loop over 5 blocks with a 4-line cache. LRU always evicts exactly the block that is needed next, so the fully associative cache misses every time, while the direct-mapped one keeps 3 of the 5 blocks in place and hits on them. Usually more associativity helps - but 'always' is the word to distrust.
